Implementation file: src/claim-office.ts
Passing tests: 23
Recent Green phase: added per-item reimbursement rates to claims. New `reimbursementRateFor(item)` returns HALF (0.5) when the item's enchantment is >= HEAVILY_ENCHANTED_LEVEL (8), else IN_FULL (1). New `reimbursableAmountOf(damage, insuredItems)` finds the damaged item in the policy's item list by matching `damage.itemType` to `item.type` and scales the damage amount by that rate. `totalDamageOf` and `payoutFor` both gained an `insuredItems` parameter to thread the policy items through.

Note: there are now two distinct enchantment thresholds with similar names — HIGH_ENCHANTMENT_LEVEL (5) for the quoting risk surcharge, and HEAVILY_ENCHANTED_LEVEL (8) for claim reimbursement. They are genuinely different business rules on the same attribute; make sure the naming keeps them distinguishable rather than merging them.

Coming next (do NOT implement): damage to an item made of dragon material is fully reimbursed even when heavily enchanted, so the rate rules will need an ordering.

Refactor the implementation while keeping all tests green. Run tests with `pnpm test`, and typecheck with `npx tsc --noEmit` (vitest does not typecheck).

Run autonomously, return when done.

content.text:
Refactoring complete. All 23 tests green, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## Naming evaluation (first priority)

Your note about the two thresholds was the main finding. `HIGH_ENCHANTMENT_LEVEL` vs `HEAVILY_ENCHANTED_LEVEL` distinguished two unrelated business rules by an adverb — "high" vs "heavy" — which is about the weakest signal available, and both names describe *the item* rather than *the rule*. Renamed to say what each level does:

- `SURCHARGEABLE_ENCHANTMENT_LEVEL = 5` — makes an item dearer to insure (quoting)
- `HALVING_ENCHANTMENT_LEVEL = 8` — makes damage cheaper to reimburse (claims)

Each carries a comment pointing at the other. The predicate `isHighlyEnchanted` became `attractsEnchantmentSurcharge`, naming the consequence rather than restating the constant. They now read as different rules at a glance, not near-synonyms.

## Rule 2 (intent): undefined lifted out of the rate rule

`reimbursementRateFor` took `InsuredItem | undefined` and used `item?.enchantment ?? 0`, so it was doing two jobs: deciding a rate, and absorbing a failed lookup. Split into `damagedItemIn` (lookup, resolves the miss to a named `UNCOVERED_ITEM`) and `reimbursementRateFor(item: InsuredItem)` (rate rules only).

This is the change that matters most for what's coming next. Dragon material needs an *ordered* rule set inside `reimbursementRateFor` — dragon wins over heavy enchantment. Adding that ordering to a function that was simultaneously handling `undefined` would have meant every new rule re-deciding what a missing item means. Now each rule reads one attribute of a real item; the uncovered case is decided once, at the lookup. `UNCOVERED_ITEM` has no `material`, so it will fall through the dragon rule to `IN_FULL` unchanged.

## Rule 3 (duplication): type matching

`areAllTheSameKind` (grouping) and the claim lookup both compared `item.type`. Extracted `isOfType(type)` as a shared predicate, used by both. Small, but it's the one concept both halves of the domain share. Note this required moving the definition above `areAllTheSameKind` — `const` arrows aren't hoisted, so the original placement would have thrown a TDZ error at runtime rather than failing the typecheck.

Also extracted `enchantmentOf(item)`, which folds the `?? 0` default that both enchantment rules were repeating independently.

## APP mass

Roughly flat: −1 (one `?.` conditional removed from `reimbursementRateFor`) +2 (the `??` in `damagedItemIn`, plus `isOfType`'s extra invocation), against −2 from the two `?? 0` defaults collapsing into `enchantmentOf`. Net ≈ −1 across the claims section.

The mass barely moved and that's the honest result here — this pass bought clarity and a cleaner seam for the next rule, not smaller code. Per Rule 2 trumping APP, I'd have taken these renames even at a mass increase.

File: `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-11_11-46-02_claim-office-prose_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`

One thing to flag for later, untouched because no test reaches it: `isFirstContractAtStep` still infers "first contract" from step index 0, which breaks for any scenario opening with a claim. The existing comment says as much. The three `it.todo` scenario tests at the bottom of the spec look likely to be what forces that fix.
